questions.problem: Determine if the vector $u$ lies on the plane $Π:r=sb+tc$, $t,s\in R$, where  $b=⟨-1,4,3⟩$, $c=⟨1,-6,-7⟩$, and  $u=⟨1,-10,-15⟩.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of $s\cdot t$ from the decomposition $u=sb+tc.$
questions.worked_solution:
By definition, $u\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -6 \\ -7\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -10 \\ -15\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-s+t=1 \\ 4s-6t=-10 \\ 3s-7t=-15\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 4 & -6 & -10 \\ 3 & -7 & -15\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & -6 \\ 3 & -7 & -15\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & -4 & -12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-s+t=1 \\ -2t=-6 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
-2t=-6\,⟹\,t=3.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-s+t & =1 \\ -s+3 & =1 \\ -s & =-2 \\ s & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=2,\,t=3,$ we conclude that $u$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
u=2b+3c.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=2\cdot 3=6.$

questions.problem:
The domain of the vector-valued function $f(t)=(t+1)\,i+\operatorname{tan}⁡(3t)\,j+{e}^{-t}\,k$ is 

$$
t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),\,t\ne \bbox[5pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAA}}.
$$

What is the missing expression? You may assume that $n$ is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the domain of $f$, we need the intersection of the domains of the individual components.

- The domain of the 1st component $t+1$ is $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

- The domain of the 2nd component $\operatorname{tan}⁡(3t)$ is $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ except for the values of $t$ for which

$$
3t=\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi n\,⟹\,t=\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi n}{3},
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

- The domain of the 3rd component ${e}^{-t}$ is $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Therefore, the domain of the vector-valued function $f(t)$ is 

$$
t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),\,t\ne \frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi n}{3},
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

questions.problem:
Find a normal vector to the plane

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 17 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -7 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+s[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,t,\,s\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
From the parametric equation, we have that $v=⟨2,-7,1⟩$ and $w=⟨3,5,0⟩$ are parallel to the plane.

Now, we need to find a normal vector of the plane. To do that, we use the cross product of $v$ and $w$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =v\times w \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -7 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\times [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & -7 & 1 \\ 3 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-5i+3j+31k \\  & =⟨-5,3,31⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨-5,3,31⟩.$

questions.problem:
Let $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 2 \\ -3 & k\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],$ where $k$ is a constant such that $k\ne -1.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $det(A)\ne 0$

II. $Ax=0$ has no solutions

III. The lines $6x+2y=1$ and $-3x+ky=-2$ intersect at infinitely many points
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that given $A=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{aligned}]$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

1\. $A$ is invertible.

2\. The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

3\. The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

4\. The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

5\. $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

- Statement I is true. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det[\begin{aligned}6 & 2 \\ -3 & k\end{aligned}] \\  & =6\cdot k-2\cdot (-3) \\  & =6k+6.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $6k+6\ne 0$ if $k\ne -1.$

Now, since the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem is true, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

- Statement II is false. According to the third part of the invertible matrix theorem, there must be a unique zero solution to $Ax=0.$

- Statement III is false. According to the fourth part of the invertible matrix theorem, the lines must intersect at exactly one point.

Finally, only statement I is true.

$x$ $0$ $1$
${f}_{X}(x)$ $0.3$ $0.7$

$y$ $-2$ $0$ $2$
${f}_{Y}(y)$ $0.6$ $0.3$ $0.1$

Which of the following statements are true? I. $P(X=0,Y=0)=P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=0)$ II. $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$ III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent
questions.worked_solution:
Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. From the table, we obtain that $P(X=0,Y=0)=f(0,0)=0.09.$ On the other hand, 

$$
P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=0)={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(0)=0.3\cdot 0.3=0.09.\,✓
$$

- Statement II is false. Checking some possible products, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,-2) & =0.16\ne 0.3\cdot 0.6={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(-2) & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $P(X=x,Y=y)\ne P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y.$

- Statement III is false. Since statement II is false, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ are *not* independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S=Z\times R$ in the Cartesian plane?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=Z\times R
$$

 
contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is an integer number and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in Z,\,y\in R\}
$$

To visualize $S,$ consider ${S}_{-1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $-1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
{S}_{-1}=\{(-1,y)\,:\,y\in R\}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{-1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14131041/assets/3fdfed680e3fb46adbe8a70aac86682aacb85d43e0675923f87658635fc89a1e.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(1,y)\,:\,y\in R\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14131041/assets/7fbda500ecca7e18c9db9939ad78d4dcc6bf488bc7fc4de1137e764ce21a0254.png)

We can create the subsets $…,{S}_{-3},{S}_{-2},{S}_{0},{S}_{2},{S}_{3},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}R\times N & =…{S}_{-2}\cup {S}_{-1}\cup {S}_{0}\cup {S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}… \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in Z}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $Z\times R$ as the set of vertical lines shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14131041/assets/4535a7c6aa7fe8f358d3463b4654c735e53df373d1001916dc035290ca54f969.png)

questions.problem:
Calculate the volume of the $4$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the vectors

$$
a=[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,c=[\begin{aligned}13 \\ 11 \\ -5 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,d=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's construct the matrix $M,$ whose columns are the coordinates of our vectors $a,$ $b,$ $c,$ and  $d:$

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 5 & 13 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 11 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -5 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The volume of the parallelepiped spanned by these vectors equals the absolute value of the determinant of $M:$

$$
V=|det(M)|
$$

The determinant of a triangular matrix is equal to the product of the entries on the main diagonal. So, we have

$$
det(M)=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 5 & 13 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 11 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -5 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=(-7)\cdot (-2)\cdot (-5)\cdot 1=-70.
$$

Therefore, the volume is

$$
V=|det(M)|=|-70|=70.
$$
